data.title: Štefanovičová: Slovakia in the Time of Svatopluk – an Archaeologist's View
data.excerpt: An attempt to assess the eastern part of Svatopluk's Moravia from an archaeologist's viewpoint runs straight into the unresolved chronology of the material evidence. Tatiana Štefanovičová weighs what the written and the material sources can say about the 9th century, and reviews the central hillforts, churches, crafts and jewellery of the territory of present-day Slovakia.

data.metaDescription: Tatiana Štefanovičová on the eastern part of Svatopluk's Moravia: the chronology of 9th-century finds, the central hillforts, churches and jewellery.

keyFacts.label: Subject
keyFacts.value: An archaeological assessment of the eastern part of Svatopluk's Moravia (present-day Slovakia)

keyFacts.label: Periodisation

timeline.title: The Blatnica–Mikulčice horizon
timeline.description: The period of material culture corresponding to the principalities of Mojmír and Pribina; its fading may reach as far as the middle of the 9th century.

timeline.title: The period of Great Moravia
timeline.description: It follows on from the Blatnica–Mikulčice horizon; the classic Great Moravian culture corresponds to it in D. Bialeková's periodisation.

timeline.title: Rastislav's accession
timeline.description: From Rastislav's accession the data of the written sources on Great Moravia multiply markedly.

timeline.title: The rise of regional centres
timeline.description: A territorial-administrative system run from several hillforts with a central function takes shape – Bratislava, Devín, Starý Tekov, Bíňa, Divinka, Vyšehrad, Zvolen-Môťová, Šarišské Sokolovce.

timeline.title: Arrival of the Byzantine mission
timeline.description: The Christianising efforts of several missions were completed by the Byzantine mission of Constantine and Methodius, active in Moravia from this year.

timeline.title: The first Magyar raids
timeline.description: The nomadic Magyar tribes were making occasional raids on Great Moravia.

timeline.title: The Magyar danger becomes acute
timeline.description: From this year the Magyars represented an acute danger, to which a Great Moravia already shorn of territory finally succumbed.

timeline.title: The end of Nitra jewellery
timeline.description: With the arrival of the Magyar tribes the production of the distinctive Nitra group of jewellery of Balkan origin comes to an end.

children.text: An attempt to assess the eastern part of Svatopluk's Moravia from the viewpoint of an archaeologist confronts us with the problems of resolving the chronology of the material source base. It is interesting to compare what written and material sources are able to tell us about the 9th century. While for the first half of the 9th century we have only very scanty written reports at our disposal, the archaeological material — thanks to the working out of the Blatnica–Mikulčice horizon — allows us to date some sites reasonably well and to form a picture of the development of the society of that time, about which the written sources tell us almost nothing. The situation in the second half of the 9th century is different. From Rastislav's accession in 846 the data of the written sources multiply, and for the time of Svatopluk's reign we can already use them to reconstruct the political and cultural development of Great Moravia. Archaeological finds are certainly no fewer — on the contrary — but their chronological placing is worse. In the periodisation of the Slavic period as presented by D. Bialeková (1980, 215), the 9th century is divided into two large periods from the point of view of both historical development and material culture: up to 830 the period of the principalities of Mojmír and Pribina, and from 830 to 910 the period of Great Moravia follows on from it. In material culture this corresponds to the Blatnica–Mikulčice horizon from 790 to 830, whose fading may reach as far as the middle of the 9th century, and it is followed by the classic Great Moravian culture, which has not been worked out in greater detail.

This failure to resolve a more detailed chronology of the Great Moravian period also causes problems in characterising Svatopluk's Moravia. Since attempts to sort pottery chronologically have so far proved unsuccessful, work is done with metal assemblages: in the earlier period with spurs and components of warrior and riding equipment, in the later period above all with jewellery. The question of the chronology of women's jewellery in the 9th century has been a problem for quite some time, as B. Dostál (1991, 81) has already pointed out. Several groups can be distinguished within it; the largest share belongs to the so-called Byzantine-Oriental jewellery. Because of its demanding artistic and technical workmanship and its frequent occurrence in precious metals, it was given attention already by J. Schránil (1925) and L. Niederle (1927), who dated it as late as the 10th–11th centuries. V. Hrubý (1955), in processing the finds from Staré Město – Na Valách, pushed this dating back, but even in his work the greater part of the finds is assigned to the last third of the 9th and the first half of the 10th century. This placing was originally adopted also by B. Dostál in his work on Middle Hillfort-period cemeteries (1966a), who named it Veligrad jewellery (DOSTÁL 1966b); at present, however, he considers that it arose earlier and faded out shortly after the demise of Great Moravia (DOSTÁL 1991). Veligrad jewellery occurs above all in the cemeteries of the higher social stratum, in the milieu of princely retinues at hillforts such as Mikulčice, Staré Město near Uherské Hradiště and Pohansko near Břeclav, or in Slovakia at Bratislava, Ducové and Bíňa. At rural cemeteries only some of its forms occur, especially grape-cluster earrings, which became very popular, though they are often found in poorer execution. At these cemeteries it is mainly the jewellery of the second large group, the so-called Danubian group, that occurs, and its dating is no less problematic. The dating of Veligrad jewellery according to V. Hrubý's classification has become so established that find assemblages are automatically dated by it, following the rule that the latest item dates the assemblage. At the hillfort in Bíňa, for instance, a grave was found with spurs of type III according to D. Bialeková (1977), which can be placed in the first half of the 9th century — spurs are a relatively sensitive chronological indicator. The other graves, however, contained silver Veligrad jewellery, and so the whole cemetery was dated to the last quarter of the 9th century, or rather to the beginning of the 10th century (HOLČÍK 1991). A similar situation occurred at Ducové, where spurs from about the third of the 9th century were likewise found in one grave, but the cemetery as a whole, and the sacral building too, are dated to the end of the 9th – beginning of the 10th century — admittedly so far only in preliminary survey publications (RUTTKAY 1972, 1978). In an overall assessment we cannot rule out the possibility that some objects may have reached the graves with a delay. The only way out of this situation lies in the analysis of the extensive Moravian cemeteries, which sometimes reach several hundred graves — Staré Město, for example, 1,400 — and in working out their vertical and horizontal stratigraphy. In Slovakia such an analysis is harder to carry out, for several reasons. At the central hillforts no extensive cemeteries have survived, because the hillforts had a continuous development and, with longer use of a cemetery, the older graves were destroyed. In Moravia, by contrast, there are several sites that remained more or less undisturbed even after the demise of Great Moravia. At Bratislava Castle, for example, of the 220 graves uncovered only 5 can be assigned to the 9th century with certainty (ŠTEFANOVIČOVÁ 1975), and at Devín Castle, of more than 300 graves only 6 (PLACHÁ – HLAVICOVÁ – KELLER 1990); the rest were later. A similar situation existed at the already mentioned Ducové. Besides, in Slovakia we so far know only cemeteries of smaller extent from the 9th century. Among the largest are the cemetery in the locality known as Za kostolom in the village of Devín with 121 graves (PLACHÁ – HLAVICOVÁ – KELLER 1990, 36 ff.) and the one at Nitra-Lupka with 91 graves (CHROPOVSKÝ 1962); Čakajovce, which has not yet been published, is probably of greater extent. The results of analyses of the more extensive Moravian assemblages would certainly be more precise, and combined with the results from Slovak sites they could fill the present gap in finds from the second third of the 9th century, which we still fill more or less intuitively. In many cases it is therefore not really possible to speak of Svatopluk's Moravia in terms of archaeological finds, but rather of the development of Moravia in the second half of the 9th century.

children.text: On the basis of both historical and archaeological data we may assume that Svatopluk took over a reasonably well-developed core territory of Moravia, both in the west and in the east. The extent of this eastern part was probably defined already by Rastislav, who could build on Mojmír's gains. Archaeological finds attest hillforts with military elements, perhaps princely retinues, around the third of the 9th century not only in south-western Slovakia — Nitra-Martinský vrch (CHROPOVSKÝ 1974), Pobedim (BIALEKOVÁ 1978) — but also in the Orava region (ČAPLOVIČ 1987, 213 ff.), in the Spiš region (JAVORSKÝ 1980, 131–135) and even in the Zemplín county — Brekov (VÍZDAL 1978, 40). We do not know whether the hillforts mentioned were annexed to the territory of Moravia by Mojmír or only by Rastislav; in any case, in the second half of the 9th century they already formed part of its core territory. Views placing the eastern frontier of Great Moravia on the Hron have long been refuted archaeologically.

children.text: Around the middle of the 9th century a territorial-administrative system began to form in the territory of present-day Slovakia, run from a number of hillforts that had a central function in a particular region. The hillfort in Bratislava can be regarded as one of these, and perhaps also Devín with the adjoining territory of Záhorie. In central Slovakia such a function was probably held by the hillfort at Starý Tekov, which initially retained its continuity in the Kingdom of Hungary as well (HABOVŠTIAK 1978, 193–195). We are not even speaking here of Nitra, which retained its privileged position not only throughout the existence of Great Moravia, but also in the beginnings of the early medieval Hungarian state. The lower Hron region was probably controlled by the hillfort at Bíňa, which was also refortified later (HABOVŠTIAK 1966). The most recently published results of the excavation at the hillfort in Mužla-Čenkov do not count it among the central hillforts, but it is an interesting record of internal Slavic colonisation after the demise of the Avar Khaganate (HANULIAK – KUZMA – ŠALKOVSKÝ 1993). In northern Slovakia another hillfort arose around the middle of the 9th century at Divinka near Žilina (MORAVČÍK 1978, 58–59). The archaeological finds so far show that it was a centre of craft production; whether it was also a tribal hillfort remains open. On the boundary between the upper Nitra region and the Turiec Basin the upland site of Vyšehrad was occupied, which may be considered the central hillfort of the Turiec Basin (REMIÁŠOVÁ 1978, 144–146). The Zvolen Basin was administered from the hillfort in the locality known as Zvolen-Môťová. In the Spiš region the function of the hillfort at Spišské Tomášovce was taken over by the nearby hillfort at Smižany (JAVORSKÝ 1978, 131–135). At this time the hillfort on Dreveník above Spišské Vlachy also came into being. The finds from it come from the 1930s and do not suggest a central function, but its position on a mountain ridge, at the opposite end of which Spiš Castle was built in the 11th century, underlines the importance of the place. In the Šariš region the hillfort at Šarišské Sokolovce served as a craft centre; it arose in the middle of the 9th century and was inhabited in the 10th–11th centuries as well (BÉREŠ 1978, 205–207). In the Zemplín region, besides Brekov, in the second half of the 9th century the Slavs occupied the originally Celtic hillfort of Zemplín, with massive fortifications, which survived as a comitatus castle in the Kingdom of Hungary as well. Although a precise dating of the origin of these hillforts is not really possible, it is very likely that they arose during Rastislav's reign, and that precisely because Svatopluk took over a principality with a firm organisational structure he was able to embark on extensive conquests, by which he substantially enlarged the original territory of Great Moravia. The lands he annexed to Moravia, whether in the west or in the east, did indeed create an extensive empire, but during his lifetime they were not so internally interconnected in organisational terms as the core of Great Moravia, which became apparent soon after his death in their falling away.

children.text: In the second half of the 9th century a great concentration of fortified sites arose in the area of Nitra, where in Svatopluk's time there was certainly a castle town, but because so few of the finds have been published the process of its formation cannot yet be outlined. In any case, in the last third of the 9th century this was an advanced form of settlement, the predecessor of the later medieval town.

Svatopluk likewise took over an already established and further developing church organisation. The beginnings of Christianisation can be sought at the start of the 9th century, when it reached the territory of present-day Slovakia through the Bavarian mission. For Slovakia this is also recorded in the mention in the Conversio of the consecration of a church at Nitra for Prince Pribina. The Christianising efforts of several missions were then completed in organisational terms by the Byzantine mission, represented by Constantine and Methodius, which was active in Moravia from 863. The written sources speak of the activity of Methodius and his disciples during Svatopluk's reign, and of Methodius's disputes with Wiching and with Svatopluk himself. The archaeological evidence has survived only in the form of the foundations of sacral buildings, or in places only as foundation trenches with minimal traces of their art-historical furnishings. The evidential value of the features themselves is therefore small; they must always be assessed in the context of the whole find situation. Dating the buildings is possible only on the basis of find associations, above all with the graves laid around them. In Slovakia four sacral buildings of the 9th century are so far materially attested — Nitra-Martinský vrch (CHROPOVSKÝ 1972), Bratislava (ŠTEFANOVIČOVÁ 1975), Ducové (RUTTKAY 1978) and Devín (PLACHÁ – HLAVICOVÁ 1981, 63–66). The as yet unpublished excavation of Nitra Castle suggests a further building. Which of the Nitra churches can be regarded as the building mentioned in the Conversio will be shown only by further research. The church on Martinský vrch, with a rectangular east end and relatively massive walls, is placed in the first half of the 9th century, also in view of the find of a coin of Charles the Bald. The construction of the rotunda at the magnate's residence in Ducové can be assumed around the middle of the 9th century, especially in view of the already mentioned grave with spurs. The three-aisled basilica at Bratislava Castle may have been built at a similar time; a more precise dating is prevented by the problems of chronology mentioned above. These buildings thus probably arose before the arrival of the Byzantine mission. Its activity may be connected with the construction of the church with a trefoil apse at Devín, on the southern side of which graves with spurs and jewellery of the second half of the 9th century were found. Whether it was built in the 860s or only in the 870s, that is, during Svatopluk's reign, cannot be determined from the finds. The hypothetically assumed Great Moravian origin of some early Romanesque buildings — for example Drážovce, Kostoľany pod Tribečom or Michalovce — has not been possible to confirm chronologically. Archaeology has certainly contributed substantially to the overall picture of the Christianisation of Great Moravia, but it says nothing about its course during Svatopluk's reign.

children.text: The archaeological sources give us a more detailed picture of the overall economic development of this period. Craft production was advanced, especially iron smelting and smithing, as shown by numerous finds of iron tools and weapons at settlements, in graves and in hoards (BIALEKOVÁ 1981). Questions of military equipment and armament were dealt with in detail by A. Ruttkay (1975, 119–216; 1976, 245–395). All the branches of craft production cannot be discussed here; I shall mention only some that are particularly conspicuous in Slovakia for this period. Among them is tar production, attested by finds of tar kilns at Bojnice and at Koš near Prievidza (BIALEKOVÁ 1962, 823–840; REMIÁŠOVÁ – RUTTKAY 1967, 455–464). Pottery deserves special attention, forming the largest percentage of finds throughout the 9th century. In the last third of the 9th century specialised pottery production is attested in the suburbium of the hillfort at Nitra-Lupka (CHROPOVSKÝ 1962). 13 pottery kilns in three batteries, with technically advanced pottery, were uncovered there. Vessels identical to those found in the kilns were also deposited in graves in the adjoining cemetery of the suburbium, where their dating was made possible by the accompanying material, above all jewellery. It may be assumed that the suburbium settlement was a service settlement of potters and that it supplied above all the princely milieu in Nitra, which, however, has not yet been identified. It also served for export, as Vlkolinská (1995) indicates on the basis of several finds. It was not in common use, for at the nearby site of Čakajovce we already find quite different, more primitive pottery from the same period.

children.text: Jewellery production was highly developed. The Veligrad jewellery already mentioned is known above all from the princely milieu of the hillforts, though this is not an absolute rule. It therefore remains a question whether it was imported into Slovakia from Moravia, as Š. Holčík (1991) believes in connection with the finds at Bíňa, or whether such jewellers' workshops existed in Slovakia as well. It occurs quite abundantly in cemeteries that continue into the 10th century, such as Trnovec nad Váhom, Holiare (TOČÍK 1971, 1968) and Ducové (RUTTKAY 1978). This suggests that it was originally first made in southern Moravia, but that goldsmiths' workshops later came into being in Slovakia as well. Here it occurs more frequently than in Bohemia, where it was evidently imported goods. In the time of Svatopluk's Moravia a new group of jewellery appears in Slovakia, named the Nitra group after the first and most distinctive find spot (CHROPOVSKÝ 1962, DOSTÁL 1966a). It has the characteristic features of Balkan jewellery, and it is likely that during Svatopluk's reign it was brought to south-western Slovakia by craftsmen from the Balkans (ŠTEFANOVIČOVÁ 1989, 215–230). Its production came to an end at the beginning of the 10th century, with the arrival of the Magyar tribes.

The expansion of Svatopluk's Moravia did not outlive its creator. The advanced central region of the empire, whose eastern part was formed by the territory of present-day Slovakia, did not manage to integrate the newly conquered territories, which were at a different level of development. The causes were internal disputes within the empire, which erupted after Svatopluk's death, but above all the external threat from the nomadic Magyar tribes, which had been making occasional raids as early as the 860s. From 896 the Magyars already represented an acute danger, to which Great Moravia — already shorn of most of the territories conquered by Svatopluk — finally succumbed, although its advanced economy and culture long survived.
